```{r packages-data, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
source(here::here("R", "slide-things.R"))

# Colors from the slide theme, all readable on white ----
clr_bar <- "#538ba2"
clr_soft <- "#c5d9e2"
clr_mean <- "#a93e31"
clr_andy <- "#244a70"
clr_dev <- "#8a6100"

theme_slides <- function(base_size = 20) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
          axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1)))
}

fmt <- function(x, d = 2) str_replace(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d), "^-", "−")
sgn <- function(x, d = 2) paste0(if_else(x < 0, "−", "+"), fmt(abs(x), d))

# Baseline scores. Treat the 619 students as a population ----
baseline <- read_csv(here::here("files", "data", "mindspark", "ms_blel_jpal_baseline.csv"),
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
math <- baseline$tot_math
hindi <- baseline$tot_hindi
n_all <- length(math)
mu <- mean(math)
sigma <- sqrt(sum((math - mu)^2) / n_all)
mu_h <- mean(hindi)
sigma_h <- sqrt(sum((hindi - mu_h)^2) / n_all)
max_m <- round(max(math / baseline$per_math, na.rm = TRUE))
max_h <- round(max(hindi / baseline$per_hindi, na.rm = TRUE))

z_of <- function(x) (x - mu) / sigma
z_math <- z_of(math)

score_pct <- tibble(score = math) %>%
  count(score) %>%
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / n_all) %>%
  complete(score = 0:26, fill = list(n = 0, pct = 0))

# Andy's score ----
andy <- 19
dev <- andy - mu
z_andy <- z_of(andy)
z_andy_h <- (andy - mu_h) / sigma_h
same_score <- sum(math == andy & hindi == andy)
share_below <- mean(math < andy)
share_below_h <- mean(hindi < andy)

# The five students from Tuesday, as a sample ----
five <- baseline$tot_math[4:8]
five_m <- mean(five)
five_sd <- sd(five)

# Squared scores, to show a change of shape ----
sq <- math^2
mu_sq <- mean(sq)
sigma_sq <- sqrt(sum((sq - mu_sq)^2) / n_all)
sq_binned <- tibble(sq = sq) %>%
  mutate(bin = floor(sq / 40) * 40 + 20) %>%
  count(bin) %>%
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / n_all)

# The bars of a histogram, with the mean and Andy marked, under any new labels ----
relabel_plot <- function(f, x_title, d = 2, y_top = 15.5) {
  label_y <- y_top * 0.93
  ggplot(score_pct, aes(x = score, y = pct)) +
    geom_col(fill = clr_soft, width = 0.85) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = mu, color = clr_mean, linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = andy, color = clr_andy, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text", x = mu - 0.3, y = label_y, label = paste("Mean:", fmt(f(mu), d)), hjust = 1,
             color = clr_mean, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
    annotate("text", x = andy + 0.3, y = label_y, label = paste("Andy:", fmt(f(andy), 0)), hjust = 0,
             color = clr_andy, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 4), labels = function(x) fmt(f(x), 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, y_top), breaks = seq(0, 15, 5)) +
    labs(x = x_title, y = "% of students") +
    theme_slides()
}
```

# z-scores and locations

---

layout: true
class: title title-1

---

# Andy scored 19. Is that good?

```{r andy-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.4, out.width="84%", fig.alt=paste0("Bar chart of baseline math scores for ", n_all, " Mindspark students, from 0 to 26 out of ", max_m, ". The bars peak near 12. A dashed vertical line marks Andy's score of 19, far out on the right side, where the bars are short.")}
ggplot(score_pct, aes(x = score, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = clr_soft, width = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = andy, color = clr_andy, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = andy + 0.3, y = 13.8, label = paste("Andy:", andy), hjust = 0,
           color = clr_andy, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 26, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 14.5)) +
  labs(x = paste0("Math score at baseline (out of ", max_m, ")"), y = "% of students") +
  theme_slides()
```

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019). `r n_all` students in Delhi.]

???

Andy isn't a real student in the data, but real students did score 19. Ask: how would you say how typical or unusual this score is? It's only 19 out of 35, so is that bad? A raw score means little until we know where the other scores are.

---

# Measure the distance in SDs

```{r ruler-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.25, out.width="82%", fig.alt=paste0("The same bar chart with a solid line at the mean of ", fmt(mu), " and a dashed line at Andy's score of 19. An arrow between them is labeled as a deviation of ", fmt(dev), " points. Above it, a ruler of two segments, each one standard deviation of ", fmt(sigma), " points long, reaches almost exactly from the mean to Andy.")}
ruler <- tibble(from = mu + 0:1 * sigma, to = mu + 1:2 * sigma)

ggplot(score_pct, aes(x = score, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = clr_soft, width = 0.85) +
  annotate("segment", x = mu, xend = mu, y = 0, yend = 19.2, color = clr_mean, linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("segment", x = andy, xend = andy, y = 0, yend = 19.2, color = clr_andy, linewidth = 1.2,
           linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = mu - 0.3, y = 18.3, label = paste("Mean:", fmt(mu)), hjust = 1,
           color = clr_mean, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  annotate("text", x = andy + 0.3, y = 18.3, label = paste("Andy:", andy), hjust = 0,
           color = clr_andy, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  annotate("segment", x = mu, xend = andy, y = 14.2, yend = 14.2, color = clr_dev, linewidth = 1.1,
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.12, "inches"), type = "closed")) +
  annotate("text", x = andy + 0.3, y = 14.2, label = paste("Deviation:", fmt(dev), "points"), hjust = 0,
           color = clr_dev, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  geom_segment(data = ruler, aes(x = from, xend = to, y = 16.8, yend = 16.8), inherit.aes = FALSE,
               color = clr_bar, linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_segment(data = tibble(x = mu + 0:2 * sigma), aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 16.1, yend = 17.5),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, color = clr_bar, linewidth = 1.6) +
  annotate("text", x = mu + c(0.5, 1.5) * sigma, y = 15.6, label = "1 SD",
           color = "#35586a", size = 6, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 26, 2), limits = c(-0.5, 27)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 19.5), breaks = seq(0, 15, 5)) +
  labs(x = paste0("Math score at baseline (out of ", max_m, ")"), y = "% of students") +
  theme_slides(19)
```

.box-inv-1.small[Each SD is `r fmt(sigma)` points. Andy's `r fmt(dev)` points are `r fmt(dev)` / `r fmt(sigma)` = `r fmt(z_andy)` SDs]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

Four questions. What's typical? The mean. How far is Andy from it? The deviation. How much do scores vary overall? The SD. So how many SDs away is he?

---

# A z-score counts SDs from the mean

$$
z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{19 - `r fmt(mu)`}{`r fmt(sigma)`} = `r fmt(z_andy)`
$$

.pull-left[
.box-inv-1.small[X − μ]

How far the score is from the mean, in points. This is the deviation from Tuesday
]

.pull-right[
.box-inv-1.small[σ]

The ruler. It says how big a step is in this distribution
]

.box-1.small[Treat the `r n_all` students as a population: μ = `r fmt(mu)` and σ = `r fmt(sigma)`]

???

The z has no units. Points divided by points. That's why it will work across different tests later today.

---

# Sign: which side. Size: how far

```{r sign-table, results="asis"}
tibble(X = c(andy, 15, 11, 5)) %>%
  mutate(`Score X` = X,
         `Deviation X − μ` = sgn(X - mu),
         z = sgn(z_of(X)),
         `In words` = c("About two SDs above the mean",
                        "About one SD above the mean",
                        "Almost exactly at the mean",
                        "About one and a half SDs below the mean")) %>%
  select(-X) %>%
  kable(format = "html", align = "ccccl", table.attr = 'class="deck-table"')
```

.box-inv-1.small[z = 0 is the mean. Most of these students sit between z = −2 and z = +2: `r round(100 * mean(abs(z_math) < 2))`% of them]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

---

# From a z-score back to a score

$$
X = \mu + z\sigma = `r fmt(mu)` + `r fmt(z_andy)` \times `r fmt(sigma)` = `r fmt(mu + z_andy * sigma)`
$$

.pull-left-3[
.box-inv-1.small[First, read the z]

.center[z = `r fmt(z_andy)`, so Andy is above the mean]
]

.pull-middle-3[
.box-inv-1.small[Then go back to points]

.center[`r fmt(z_andy)` × `r fmt(sigma)` = `r fmt(dev)` points away]
]

.pull-right-3[
.box-inv-1.small[Last, add the mean]

.center[`r fmt(mu)` + `r fmt(dev)` = `r fmt(andy)`]
]

???

If you round z to 2, you get `r fmt(mu + 2 * sigma)`, not 19. Keep two decimals along the way. The lab and the homework will say how much to round.

---

# A sample works the same way

```{r formula-table, results="asis"}
tribble(
  ~` `, ~`Score to z`, ~`z to score`,
  "Population", "\\(z = \\dfrac{X - \\mu}{\\sigma}\\)", "\\(X = \\mu + z\\sigma\\)",
  "Sample", "\\(z = \\dfrac{X - M}{\\hat{\\sigma}}\\)", "\\(X = M + z\\hat{\\sigma}\\)"
) %>%
  kable(format = "html", align = "lcc", escape = FALSE, table.attr = 'class="deck-table"')
```

.box-inv-1.small[
Tuesday's five: M = `r fmt(five_m, 1)` and σ̂ = `r fmt(five_sd)`. In this sample, the `r max(five)` has z = `r fmt((max(five) - five_m) / five_sd)`
]

.book-tag[
In the book: σ̂ is written s
]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

Same idea, different symbols. Greek means population, and a Latin letter or a hat means an estimate. A z-score in a sample uses the estimates.

---

class: title title-8

# Try it: Answer

.pull-left-3[
.box-inv-8.medium[Question 1]

.center[(9 − `r fmt(mu)`) / `r fmt(sigma)` = **`r fmt(z_of(9))`**]
]

.pull-middle-3[
.box-inv-8.medium[Question 2]

.center[`r fmt(mu)` + 1.50 × `r fmt(sigma)` = **`r fmt(mu + 1.5 * sigma)`**]
]

.pull-right-3[
.box-inv-8.medium[Question 3]

.center[(`r min(five)` − `r fmt(five_m, 1)`) / `r fmt(five_sd)` = **`r fmt((min(five) - five_m) / five_sd)`**]
]

.box-8.small[A negative z-score means below the mean. It doesn't mean a bad score]

class: center middle section-title section-title-6 animated fadeIn

# Transforming distributions

---

layout: true
class: title title-6

---

# A 19 means nothing by itself

```{r twelve-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.2, out.width="84%", fig.alt="Bar chart of baseline math scores with the mean and Andy's score of 19 marked by vertical lines."}
relabel_plot(identity, paste0("Math score at baseline (out of ", max_m, ")"))
```

.box-inv-6.small[It's only a label. We could relabel every score, and everyone would keep their place]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

---

# Subtract 10: the labels slide

```{r minus-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.2, out.width="84%", fig.alt=paste0("The same bars with a new axis, running from −10 to 14. The mean is now ", fmt(mu - 10), " and Andy's score is now ", andy - 10, ". The picture is the same.")}
relabel_plot(function(x) x - 10, "Score − 10")
```

.box-inv-6.small[Mean: `r fmt(mu)` → `r fmt(mu - 10)`. The SD stays at `r fmt(sigma)`. Andy is still `r fmt(z_andy)` SDs above the mean]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

---

# Multiply by 10: the labels stretch

```{r times-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.2, out.width="84%", fig.alt=paste0("The same bars with a new axis, running from 0 to 240. The mean is now ", fmt(mu * 10, 1), " and Andy's score is now ", andy * 10, ". The picture is the same.")}
relabel_plot(function(x) x * 10, "Score × 10", d = 1)
```

.box-inv-6.small[Mean: `r fmt(mu)` → `r fmt(mu * 10, 1)`. SD: `r fmt(sigma)` → `r fmt(sigma * 10, 1)`. Andy is still `r fmt(z_andy)` SDs above the mean]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

---

# Do both: subtract, then multiply

```{r both-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.2, out.width="84%", fig.alt=paste0("The same bars with a new axis, running from −100 to 140. The mean is now ", fmt((mu - 10) * 10, 1), " and Andy's score is now ", (andy - 10) * 10, ". The picture is the same.")}
relabel_plot(function(x) (x - 10) * 10, "(Score − 10) × 10", d = 1)
```

.box-inv-6.small[Mean: `r fmt(mu)` → `r fmt((mu - 10) * 10, 1)`. SD: `r fmt(sigma)` → `r fmt(sigma * 10, 1)`. Andy is still `r fmt(z_andy)` SDs above the mean]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

---

# These only change the labels

```{r rules-table, results="asis"}
tribble(
  ~`Do this to every score`, ~Mean, ~SD, ~Shape,
  "Add or subtract a constant", "Moves by the constant", "Stays the same", "Stays the same",
  "Multiply or divide by a positive constant", "Multiplied or divided", "Multiplied or divided", "Stays the same"
) %>%
  kable(format = "html", align = "lccc", table.attr = 'class="deck-table"')
```

.box-6.small.sp-after-half[We call these "scale-invariant" transformations]

.box-inv-6.small[They keep the shape and the relative distances between students]

???

The SD ignores a shift because it's built from distances between scores and the mean. Both move together, so the distances don't change.

---

# Squaring changes the shape

```{r square-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.9, out.width="88%", fig.alt="Two bar charts. The left one shows math scores, close to symmetric. The right one shows the same scores squared, with a peak near 140 and a long tail to the right."}
bind_rows(
  score_pct %>% transmute(x = score, pct, panel = "Math score", w = 0.85),
  sq_binned %>% transmute(x = bin, pct, panel = "Math score squared", w = 34)
) %>%
  mutate(panel = fct_inorder(panel)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = pct, width = w)) +
  geom_col(fill = clr_bar) +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of students") +
  theme_slides(19)
```

.box-inv-6.small[Now 4 and 6 are 20 apart, but 18 and 20 are 76 apart]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

Not every transformation is a relabeling. Both pairs of students were 2 points apart. After squaring, 4 and 6 become 16 and 36, while 18 and 20 become 324 and 400. So this isn't a relabeling. It changed who is close to whom.

---

# Standardized distributions

---

layout: true
class: title title-3

---

# A z-score is the same kind of relabeling

$$
z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}
$$

.pull-left[
.box-inv-3.small[Subtract one constant]

That constant is the mean
]

.pull-right[
.box-inv-3.small[Divide by another constant]

That constant is the standard deviation
]

.box-3.small[Do it to every score and you get a *standardized* distribution]

---

# Same picture, new axis: mean 0, SD 1

```{r z-axis-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.3, out.width="84%", fig.alt=paste0("The same bars of math scores with two axes. The bottom axis shows raw scores. The top axis shows z-scores from −3 to 4, with 0 at the mean of ", fmt(mu), ". Andy's score of 19 lines up with a z-score of ", fmt(z_andy), ".")}
ggplot(score_pct, aes(x = score, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = clr_soft, width = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu + c(-2, -1, 1) * sigma, color = "#8d99a5", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu, color = clr_mean, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = andy, color = clr_andy, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = andy + 0.3, y = 13.8, label = paste("Andy: z =", fmt(z_andy)), hjust = 0,
           color = clr_andy, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  annotate("text", x = mu + 0.3, y = 13.8, label = "z = 0", hjust = 0,
           color = clr_mean, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 26, 2), limits = c(-0.6, 27),
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ z_of(.), breaks = -3:4, name = "z-score",
                                         labels = function(x) fmt(x, 0))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 14.5)) +
  labs(x = "Math score at baseline", y = "% of students") +
  theme_slides()
```

.box-inv-3.small[The z-scores have mean `r fmt(abs(round(mean(z_math), 2)))` and SD `r fmt(sqrt(mean(z_math^2)))`. Every student keeps their place]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

The book draws this with a normal curve. Here it's the real data. Nothing moved: we printed a second ruler on the plot.

---

# z-scores don't make a shape normal

```{r shape-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.9, out.width="88%", fig.alt="Two bar charts with the same right-skewed shape. The left one shows the squared math scores on their own axis. The right one shows the same values after standardizing, with mean 0 and SD 1. The shape is identical."}
shape_data <- bind_rows(
  sq_binned %>% transmute(x = bin, pct, panel = "Squared scores", w = 34),
  sq_binned %>% transmute(x = (bin - mu_sq) / sigma_sq, pct, panel = "Squared scores, standardized", w = 34 / sigma_sq)
) %>%
  mutate(panel = fct_inorder(panel))

shape_notes <- tibble(
  panel = factor(c("Squared scores", "Squared scores, standardized"), levels = levels(shape_data$panel)),
  x = c(310, (310 - mu_sq) / sigma_sq), y = 15,
  label = c(paste0("Mean ", fmt(mu_sq, 1), ", SD ", fmt(sigma_sq, 1)), "Mean 0, SD 1")
)

ggplot(shape_data, aes(x = x, y = pct, width = w)) +
  geom_col(fill = clr_bar) +
  geom_text(data = shape_notes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0,
            color = clr_mean, size = 6, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of students") +
  theme_slides(19)
```

.box-inv-3.small[A skewed distribution stays skewed. Only the axis changes]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

This is a common mistake. Standardizing moves the center and sets the spread. It can't touch the shape. Math scores look bell-shaped because they already were.

---

# We can add labels we like better

$$
\text{New score} = \text{new mean} + z \times \text{new SD}
$$

.pull-left[
.box-inv-3.small[Mean 500, SD 100]

.center[Andy: 500 + `r fmt(z_andy)` × 100 = **`r fmt(500 + round(z_andy, 2) * 100, 0)`**]
]

.pull-right[
.box-inv-3.small[Mean 100, SD 15]

.center[Andy: 100 + `r fmt(z_andy)` × 15 = **`r fmt(100 + round(z_andy, 2) * 15, 0)`**]
]

.box-3.small[Same student, same place. Nobody needs to see a negative score or a decimal]

???

Why not stop at z? People don't like being told their score is −0.54. So test makers go one step further. It's one more scale-invariant transformation.

---

# Score reports are tables like this one

```{r report-table, results="asis"}
tibble(X = c(3, 7, 11, 15, 19)) %>%
  mutate(`Math score` = X,
         z = sgn(z_of(X)),
         `Mean 500, SD 100` = fmt(500 + 100 * z_of(X), 0),
         `Mean 100, SD 15` = fmt(100 + 15 * z_of(X), 0),
         `% who scored lower` = fmt(100 * map_dbl(X, ~ mean(math < .x)), 0)) %>%
  select(-X) %>%
  kable(format = "html", align = "c", table.attr = 'class="deck-table tight"')
```

.box-inv-3.small[The study's scaled math scores do this too: mean `r fmt(abs(round(mean(baseline$m_theta_eap, na.rm = TRUE), 2)))`, SD `r fmt(sd(baseline$m_theta_eap, na.rm = TRUE))` at baseline]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

Tests like the SAT and GRE report a scaled score and a percentile. Each testing program picks its own scale, and the percentile comes from the people who took it.

The study's scaled scores come from a measurement model, not from this simple formula. The idea of reporting in SDs is the same. Don't go further than that unless someone asks.

---

# A 19 in math beats a 19 in Hindi

```{r compare-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.9, out.width="86%", fig.alt=paste0("Two bar charts of baseline scores, on the same axis. Math has mean ", fmt(mu), " and SD ", fmt(sigma), ", and a score of 19 has a z-score of ", fmt(z_andy), ", far in the right tail. Hindi has mean ", fmt(mu_h), " and SD ", fmt(sigma_h), ", and a score of 19 has a z-score of ", fmt(z_andy_h), ", closer to the middle.")}
labels_two <- c(paste0("Math: mean ", fmt(mu), ", SD ", fmt(sigma)),
                paste0("Hindi: mean ", fmt(mu_h), ", SD ", fmt(sigma_h)))

two_tests <- tibble(score = c(math, hindi), test = rep(labels_two, each = n_all)) %>%
  mutate(test = factor(test, levels = labels_two)) %>%
  count(test, score) %>%
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / n_all)

mark_two <- tibble(test = factor(labels_two, levels = labels_two),
                   label = paste("Andy: z =", fmt(c(z_andy, z_andy_h))))

ggplot(two_tests, aes(x = score, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = clr_soft, width = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = andy, color = clr_andy, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(data = mark_two, aes(x = andy + 0.4, y = 11.5, label = label), inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0,
            color = clr_andy, size = 6, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  facet_wrap(vars(test), nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, 5), limits = c(-0.6, 33)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 5)) +
  labs(x = "Score at baseline", y = "% of students") +
  theme_slides(19)
```

.box-inv-3.small[Percent correct says Hindi: `r round(100 * andy / max_h)`% against `r round(100 * andy / max_m)`%. z-scores say math: `r fmt(z_andy)` against `r fmt(z_andy_h)`]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

Ask first: which test did Andy do better on? The tests differ in length, average and spread, so raw scores can't be compared. z-scores have no units, so they can. `r same_score` real students scored 19 on both tests.

Andy beat `r round(100 * share_below)`% of students in math and `r round(100 * share_below_h)`% in Hindi.

---

# The blueprint starts here

```{r sim-one-score, results="asis"}
sim_frame(
  alt = "Simulator at step 1. It draws one score at a time from a normal population, converts each to a z-score, and stacks the z-scores into a bell shape centered at 0",
  step = 1, mu = fmt(mu), sd = fmt(sigma), view = "stat", draws = 300, height = 490
)
```

.source[Simulator after Kristoffer Magnusson, rpsychologist.com.]

???

Click to draw a few times. Panel 1 is the population, a smooth curve with our test's mean and SD. Panel 2 is one score and its z. Panel 3 stacks the z-scores. This is step 1 of the blueprint, and every test later in the course has these three panels. Ignore the cutoffs and the p for now. They arrive with hypothesis testing.
